$comment: Two kinds of budget, and the difference decides what a failure means.
regressionThreshold is relative: a median or p95 may not exceed the checked-in
baseline.json by more than this fraction on the same environment profile. It
started at 0.2 while the harness had no run history, and is now 0.1, narrowed
the way that comment said to narrow it: after Phases 0 and 4 through 6 had put
enough gated runs on the record to show the spread. Those runs reported their
references within 1.00x to 1.17x and no render workload moved more than a few
percent between two runs of identical code, so ten percent still sits above the
noise this harness shows while halving what a real slowdown has to be before the
gate sees it. Narrow it further only against more evidence, and do not widen it
to make a red run pass — a run that reds at ten percent on a busy machine is a
run to repeat, and the maxRunSpread check below is what tells the two apart.
This threshold is the safe knob, and the reason is in measure.mjs: it is applied
to a baseline scaled by how much slower the machine is now, and a change must
also clear the minDelta slack below. A product limit has neither correction.
suiteThresholds overrides that per suite, and only the tooling suite needs it: a
workload that starts a fresh compiler process on a machine somebody is also using
does not repeat to twenty percent. Measured on this machine, three consecutive
runs of the same unchanged repository reported 3.3 s, 4.9 s and 6.0 s for the
type-aware lint, purely from concurrent load. So the tooling gate is set to catch
the order-of-magnitude change — a compiler state reuse that halves the template
check, a change that triples the typecheck — and nothing finer. Tightening it
needs a quiet machine or a dedicated runner, not a smaller number here.
minDelta is per unit, and it is why a 0.1 ms workload cannot regress. Chrome
quantises performance.now() to 100 microseconds, so a sub-millisecond median is
one or two ticks and a percentage between them is arithmetic on noise; a 1.4 ms
compile measuring 1.6 ms is the same story one tick up. A regression has to clear
both the relative threshold and this absolute slack. The same applies to bytes and
counts: heap growth of 400 KB after fifty route cycles is the collector's
discretion rather than a leak, and the batch-by-batch check in
tools/benchmark/node/lifecycle.mjs is what actually watches for one.
depth is the exception among the units, and it has its own because it must not
inherit the slack of count. A request total moves by twenty on noise; a chain
depth does not move at all unless the code that discovers those requests changed,
so its slack is 1 and a single added serial hop is a regression. It is also not
scaled by the machine, because nothing but ms is: how many requests waited for
another request is a property of the graph, not of the hardware. ADR-0082.
product is absolute: workload id -> metric -> hard limit, derived from the target
application and its hardware rather than from a previous run. It carries exactly
one entry, and the reason no timing joins it is unchanged. A product limit is
compared raw: no speed scaling, no minDelta slack, and it fails a run that the
spread check already refused to gate. Duration limits set near this machine's
medians would therefore red-build on any slower machine and on every busy moment
here — the population measured at 1.46x to 2.63x below — and a gate that reds for
the environment teaches people to ignore it. Absolute duration limits belong to a
known target machine and a known target application scale. Neither is fixed yet,
so the relative gate carries that work.
delivery/artifact-size.chainDepth is the one limit those rules already permit,
and it is not a timing. It is how many round trips deep the entry's static chunk
graph is, derived by the build from chunks[].imports, admitted by parseReport
against the graph it was derived from, and read here from a verified report
without starting a browser. A count of hops does not change with the machine, so
it needs neither the speed scaling nor the noise slack that make an absolute
duration unfair. 3 is what the example artifact builds today; raising it is a
decision to ship a deeper startup graph, taken deliberately and not as a side
effect. It applies to the dist origin alone: the source origin ships no bundler
and the browser walks the native module graph, where depth describes the source
layout rather than a delivery defect. ADR-0082.
One consequence to keep visible: no timing carries a required budget, so the table
windowing question stays unasked rather than answered. That
is intended. Windowing justified by a budget invented to justify it is the wrong
way round.
maxSpeedDrift is where scaling stops being credible. A machine twice as slow as the
one that recorded the baseline is a different machine, and its numbers are reported
as incomparable rather than divided into agreement.
maxRunSpread is the same judgement applied inside one run. A reference reading is
taken before each suite and once at the end, and if two of them disagree by more
than this the machine changed while it was being measured — a video started, an
indexer woke up — so the run reports differences, fails nothing, and refuses to
become a baseline. The reason it exists is measured: a ci run whose arithmetic
reference reported the machine unchanged at 1.01x reported seventeen regressions of
45-75% across every render and tooling workload, because the load that caused them
was in the renderer and in the page cache, where a register-only loop cannot see it.
1.25 is provisional and sits between the two populations measured on this machine:
quiet ci runs spread 1.00x to 1.14x, and runs made while a second browser was busy
spread 1.46x, 1.55x, 2.35x and 2.63x. It is a limit on the environment, not on the
repository, so tighten it on a dedicated runner rather than widening it here.
ciMaxSeconds bounds the gate. Overrunning it fails the run, so the suite cannot
grow into something that gets skipped. The ci profile currently takes about 105 s on
a quiet machine, of which about 5 s is the reference readings.
